job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in robotics in Munich, after a mechanical engineering degree. My mornings are control systems lectures, and afternoons I'm in the lab tuning a small robot arm that's supposed to sort bolts. Last summer I interned at an auto-parts maker near Stuttgart, working on a quality-inspection station. I live in student housing, call my grandmother in Osaka on Sundays, and play football on Wednesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shrug and say it's another tool in the box. In the lab, we'd say that's what the last wave of automation said too. To my grandmother I'd say nothing, because she wouldn't want it explained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel fine. Robotics engineers stay in demand when the tools are modest, and my internship firm already mentioned an opening. I use an AI helper now and then for code comments, but I don't depend on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, say yes to the parts maker if the offer comes, and keep a part of my savings in a broad index fund. I'd also finish the open-source robot-arm project I'm helping with, since it'd look good on a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I like that my plans mostly stay as I wrote them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about the claim that it's all hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's partly hype, but not all of it. I've seen the inspection software at the parts maker catch defects my supervisor would miss. A plateau doesn't mean nothing works, it means we don't get the sci-fi version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone around you who is worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle in Osaka runs a small tool-and-die shop and he's already short of apprentices. For him, a plateau is fine, because he can't hire anyway. He says the real problem is that young people don't want to touch metal.

say: I'd say it's **another tool** in the box and the last wave of automation said the same.
I'd tell my grandmother **nothing**, because she wouldn't want it explained.
think: I feel **fine**, since robotics engineers stay in demand when the tools are modest.
My internship firm already mentioned an **opening**.
do: Finish the master's and say yes to the **parts maker** if the offer comes.
Finish the **open-source** robot-arm project and hold some savings in an index fund.
feel: I feel **steady**, because plans mostly stay as I wrote them.
S0.quote: A plateau doesn't mean nothing works, it means we don't get the sci-fi version.
fieldNote: Wei is **secure**: robotics sits on the hands-on side and he has a firm opening.
His view is balanced; the plateau means no sci-fi version, not no change.
He mentions his uncle's lack of apprentices as the real labour problem.

steps.text: Accept the auto-parts maker's offer if it arrives by spring
Finish the open-source robot-arm project before graduating
Put part of my savings into a broad index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real but manageable. At the lab I'd say software engineers will feel it first and we'll get a few years. To friends I'd say learn to work with these tools because they'll be part of the job, not take the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a bit torn. The robotics software side, writing control code and tests, is exactly what AI helps with and might do on its own. The hardware side, wiring, calibrating, standing next to the machine, holds for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI helper more seriously for code, and I'd learn the vendor's inspection-software tools. I'd lean towards roles at the plant that mix both, like commissioning, which is hands-on and system-heavy. I'd also take a short course on industrial safety rules, since rules will matter more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long period of adjusting rather than a shock. I'm a bit uneasy, mostly about the juniors who write code all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why commissioning in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Commissioning means arriving at the customer's factory when a new line goes in and getting it to work. It involves people, cables and surprises. Software can plan it, but it can't stand on a noisy factory floor and decide what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How might your own job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine reports and test scripts would be written by a model, so I'd review rather than write. I'd probably get promoted faster, honestly, because the boring bits vanish. But fewer juniors might be hired, which worries me for the next group.

say: I'd say it's **real but manageable** and software engineers will feel it first.
I'd tell friends to work **with** these tools, not against them.
think: Writing control code and tests is exactly what AI helps with, while **hardware** work holds longer.
Fewer **juniors** might be hired, which worries me for the next group.
do: Use the AI helper more seriously and learn the vendor's **inspection software**.
Aim for **commissioning** roles at the plant and take a short industrial safety course.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but not shocked, mostly about juniors who write code all day.
S1.quote: Software can plan it, but it can't stand on a noisy factory floor and decide what to do.
fieldNote: Wei is **uneasy**, and his answer is to move toward hardware-and-software hybrids.
He sees routine writing becoming review, which could speed his own career.
His concern is for next year's juniors, not himself.

steps.text: Use the AI helper for control code and test scripts
Learn the vendor's inspection software during the master's
Apply for commissioning engineer roles at the auto-parts maker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is quick. I'd say governments and firms have to talk to each other now, with safety rules for robots in factories and a transition fund for workers. To friends I'd say stay flexible and don't bet on one job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Thinking tasks, including most of my software work, go in 2028, which is before I've had a real job. The hands-on robots come about 2031, so I'd be in a gap where my own field is being built by AI and then sold back to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd accept the first good offer rather than finishing the master's if the market tightens. I'd build up my savings quickly, keep living cheaply, and look for work in factory commissioning, where people still travel and install. I'd also ask my grandmother to hold off selling her flat, since her pension could be hit by a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a bridge in fog. You know the other side exists, you just can't see it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm okay for the next year because I have savings and a place to stay. But I'd also say I might need to move cities for work. They'd say come home, and I'd say maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Germany?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a plant in Japan or the US was hiring, probably yes, for a few years. Robots will be built wherever the factories are, and the factories will not wait for me to feel ready.

say: I'd say governments and firms must agree **safety rules** and a transition fund.
I'd tell friends **not to bet** on one job title.
think: Software work goes in 2028, before I've had a **real job**.
In the gap AI builds my field and **sells it back** to me.
do: Accept the first good **offer** if the market tightens, even before finishing.
Build **savings** fast and look at commissioning work, even abroad.
feel: I feel like I'm on a **bridge in fog**: the other side exists but I can't see it.
S2.quote: Robots will be built wherever the factories are, and the factories will not wait for me to feel ready.
fieldNote: Wei is **anxious** but mobile: he'd travel and relocate for work.
His savings and flexible attitude keep the anxiety from becoming alarm.
He worries about his grandmother's pension.

steps.text: Take the first good job offer before the master's ends
Save most of my pay and keep living cheaply
Look at commissioning jobs in Japan or the US

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a reasonable runway. I'd say we should spend it training people for the roles that remain: installation, maintenance, safety. I'd tell friends to do the same and not to wait for a clearer signal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but practical. By 2031 I'd have three years of experience, which is worth more than a new graduate's degree. The hands-on robots come around 2034, so the commissioning and maintenance side should hold until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as a commissioning engineer for three years and learn every part of the line. I'd learn the AI tools for planning and reports and take a project management course. I'd save about a quarter of my pay and put some into a flat in Munich or Stuttgart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long exam week. You study, you sit, you hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into maintenance and training of the robot systems themselves, or into safety auditing. Someone has to certify the robots, and that's a human job for a while. I'd also think about teaching, because my uncle's right that young people need hands-on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever start your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in my thirties. A small shop that installs and services robots for small factories, like my uncle's. The big firms ignore small factories, and they'd pay for someone who speaks both languages.

say: I'd say we should train people for the roles that remain: **installation, maintenance, safety**.
I'd tell friends to start now and not wait for a **clearer signal**.
think: By 2031 three years of **experience** is worth more than a new graduate's degree.
Commissioning and maintenance should hold until the hands-on **robots** arrive around 2034.
do: Work as a **commissioning engineer** for three years and learn every part of the line.
Take a **project management** course and save about a quarter of my pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but practical, like a long exam week.
S3.quote: The big firms ignore small factories, and they'd pay for someone who speaks both languages.
fieldNote: Wei sees a **runway** and plans around experience-before-robots.
He identifies a future niche: certifying and servicing robots for small factories.
His uncle's shop gives him a concrete picture of the future.

steps.text: Work three years as a commissioning engineer on new production lines
Take a project management course in the evenings
Save a quarter of my pay towards a flat
Use AI tools for planning and reports at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a luxury. I'd say we should use it to rebuild apprenticeships and technical training so people can move into the new jobs. I'd say it in the lab and to my uncle, who'd agree loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. By 2036 I'd be 34 with ten years in robotics, and I'd likely be training the next group. The hands-on robots around 2039 are the very systems I'd be working on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at a manufacturer for four or five years, then switch to a role at a robot maker or a safety lab. I'd keep learning the AI tools gradually, and take a year in Japan to work with my uncle's world. I'd get married around 30, if things work out, and buy a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels light and kind of exciting. I'd be building the thing that others worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it bother you to be on the building side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. If I build the robots that take someone's job at my uncle's shop, that's not a clean conscience. I'd want to build things that help small shops, not just big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who's decided to ignore all of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but keep your skills fresh. Ten years is long, and the people who do best will be the ones who didn't coast. I'd also say call your grandmother more, which isn't about work, but it's good advice.

say: I'd say we should rebuild **apprenticeships** and technical training over the decade.
I'd say it in the lab and to my uncle, who'd **agree loudly**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 and likely **training** the next group.
I'd be building the thing others worry about, which isn't a **clean conscience**.
do: Work four or five years at a manufacturer, then move to a **robot maker** or safety lab.
Spend a year in **Japan** with my uncle's world and buy a flat.
feel: I feel **light** and a little excited, with a pinch of guilt.
S4.quote: If I build the robots that take someone's job at my uncle's shop, that's not a clean conscience.
fieldNote: Wei's calm in the ten-year world comes with a **moral wrinkle** about building robots that displace people.
He links his future to his uncle's small shop and small firms.
He plans family and house alongside career.

steps.text: Work four years at a manufacturer, then join a robot maker
Spend a year in Japan helping my uncle's workshop
Buy a flat near work around age thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to get real experience before the thinking side of my field is automated. What would help is a transition fund for graduates and clear safety rules for robots in factories. I'd also want companies to hire juniors for hands-on training and not only for code.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that I'm in an odd position: I study the thing that worries everyone else. Sometimes I feel like a carpenter being asked how they feel about hammers.

headlineQuote: Sometimes I feel like a carpenter being asked how they feel about hammers.
portrait: Wei is 24, doing a **robotics** master's in Munich after a mechanical engineering degree and an auto-parts internship.
His centre outlook is pragmatic, and he uses AI tools now and then without relying on them.
He leans toward **hands-on hybrid** work like commissioning, where people still travel and install.
In the two-year world he is anxious but flexible and willing to relocate.
He worries about the **conscience** of building robots that replace people like his uncle.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because he wouldn't gain real experience before the thinking side of his field is automated.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition fund** for graduates, clear safety rules for factory robots and juniors hired for hands-on training.
